articles.title: What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?
articles.dek: At a campaign rally , in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026, President Donald Trump accused U. S.
paragraphs: At a campaign rally , in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026, President Donald Trump accused U. S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist” who wants to impose Sharia law – Islamic law – in the United States. His comments reflect a broader pattern among Republican politicians of portraying Sharia as a threat to the American legal system.

In March 2026, Texas legislators launched the Sharia Free Texas Caucus, a group dedicated to preventing what its members describe as the spread of Islamic law in Texas. Its founder, state Rep. Brent Money, has characterized Sharia as “an entire civilizational legal structure” that threatens American law and institutions. That same month, nearly 95% of Texas Republican primary voters backed a nonbinding proposition declaring that “ Texas should prohibit Sharia Law .” The movement extends beyond Texas. In Congress, the Sharia Free America Caucus , established in December 2025, grew to 68 Republican lawmakers from 25 states in just six months.
These efforts reflect a long-standing claim , frequently invoked by anti-Sharia activists, that Muslims are seeking to establish a parallel legal system that will eventually replace American law.
But this rhetoric raises a more basic question: What exactly is Sharia, and what does it actually mean for Muslims to follow it while living in the United States?

I am a law professor who studies religious liberty . My 2019 book, “ When Islam Is Not a Religion ,” examined how ordinary Muslim religious practices come to be treated as political threats, and I recently documented that pattern in Texas . The Sharia controversy shows how this happens.

In Arabic, “sharia” means a path or way, literally “ the path to a watering place .” For Muslims, it refers to the divinely ordained way of living a moral and religious life, guided by the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad.

Sharia guides Muslims how to pray, when to fast, what to eat and how much to give to charity. It also addresses marriage and divorce. These rules span what Americans would sort into law, ethics, manners and worship, as law professor and an authority on Islamic law Asifa Quraishi-Landes has explained .

This distinction matters because Americans often think of law as something established and enforced by the state. Sharia is broader than that. A Muslim who avoids pork or prays five times a day may see each practice as part of following Sharia, but neither requires a separate legal court or government enforcement.

Rules governing marriage, divorce and inheritance, by contrast, may have legal consequences, though how they are interpreted and applied varies across Islamic traditions. Indeed, as Quraishi-Landes notes, Sharia itself obliges Muslims to follow the law of the land wherever they live.

Muslims do not all agree on how Sharia should be interpreted. They distinguish between Sharia, which they regard as the divine ideal, and “ fiqh,” the human effort to understand and apply it . In other words, Muslims believe Sharia comes from God, but people must figure out what it requires in practice. Because people can disagree, interpretations can differ and change over time.
Sunni Islam’s four major schools and Shiite Islam’s legal traditions sometimes reach different conclusions about matters such as marriage, divorce and financial transactions.

For example, scholars differ on whether Muslims can take out conventional mortgages to buy homes, given Islamic prohibitions on interest, and on the conditions under which a marriage can be dissolved. They continue to debate newer questions, too, such as whether organ donation is permissible or how modern banking can comply with Islamic principles .

No single institution speaks for all Muslims. Yet political debates often treat Sharia as a fixed rule book, when much of the Islamic legal tradition consists of ongoing disagreements about what its rules mean and how they should apply.

Muslims are subject to the same laws as everyone else in the United States. Their religious commitments may guide personal decisions about marriage, divorce, finances and everyday conduct, but Sharia has no independent legal authority. Muslims can follow religious rules voluntarily, but those rules cannot override American law.

This is not unique to Islam. Religious communities across the country have long used their own procedures to resolve disputes. For example, many Orthodox Jewish couples sign prenuptial agreements committing them to appear before a Jewish religious court, known as a beth din, if their marriage breaks down. The court can then help facilitate a religious divorce, including addressing situations in which a husband refuses to grant his wife a religious divorce. Christian organizations likewise offer biblical mediation and arbitration to resolve conflicts according to religious principles.

Muslims can similarly turn to religious scholars or mediators for guidance on family or financial disputes. These arrangements are generally voluntary, and any legally enforceable agreement must comply with American law.

A religious ruling does not become binding simply because a religious authority issues it. Like other religious communities, Muslims may organize aspects of their personal lives around their faith, but they do so within the framework of American law.
Critics often claim Sharia is gaining a foothold in the courts. The concern usually arises when Muslims ask a court to recognize a religious contract or arbitration.

Consider an Islamic marriage contract promising the wife a marriage gift, known as “mahr,” some or all of which may be payable if the couple divorces. A court asked to enforce it does not decide what Islamic theology requires. It asks whether the agreement meets ordinary contract law. In 2020, a Maryland appeals court held that a “mahr” could be enforced only under the same secular standards that apply to any agreement between spouses. In other words, the court’s job is to determine whether the couple’s agreement is legally enforceable, just as it would with any other contract. It is not enforcing Islamic religious law.

Courts may apply what the Supreme Court calls “ neutral principles of law .” That simply means applying ordinary legal rules without deciding religious questions. A judge can determine whether two people entered into a valid contract, for example, but cannot decide which interpretation of Islam is religiously correct. As law professor Haider Ala Hamoudi has observed , courts can enforce a “mahr” agreement precisely because doing so does not require them to interpret Islamic law.

Arbitration works the same way. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has called Islamic panels “ Sharia tribunals masquerading as legal courts .” Yet the Beth Din of America also structures its proceedings so civil courts can enforce its rulings, as do Christian arbitrators.

Courts can enforce voluntary arbitration awards and can also vacate them for fraud or overreach. For example, suppose a Muslim couple voluntarily agree to have a religious arbitrator resolve a financial dispute. If the arbitrator orders one spouse to pay the other US$10,000, a court may enforce that decision just as it would any other arbitration award. But if one spouse was coerced into participating or the arbitrator exceeded the authority the couple had agreed to give them, a court could set the decision aside.
A religious arbitrator cannot override a statute or the Constitution.

Some concerns stem from how certain governments enforce Islamic law. In Iran, U. N. investigators have documented escalating violence against women accused of violating hijab rules. In Afghanistan, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees targeting women and girls .

articles.title: Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate
articles.dek: Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily…
paragraphs: Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own , further cementing those views.
But this research often omits an important source of political information: popular culture , from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies.

Politics are intertwined with popular entertainment media . The current president is a former reality television star who was reelected in 2024 with the help of comedy podcasters like Joe Rogan . Blockbuster films such as “The Odyssey” spark controversy and turn into political footballs , while late-night talk show hosts must skirt the Trump administration’s regulatory ire with their politically oriented humor.

While we know a lot about the news-consumption habits of Republicans and Democrats , there is less data about the other places that people encounter political ideas. This is particularly true for younger people, who are increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers and popular culture sources .

Political consultant Sarah Longwell of The Bulwark recently told The New York Times’ Ezra Klein that many people in her focus groups get political information from an “algorithm-driven information environment” populated by influencers, comedians and sports personalities. She noted that the “overlap between politics and culture” creates a “vibe” that shapes many people’s political decision-making.

As co-founders and research affiliates of Colorado State University’s Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture , we conducted a survey that documents the pop culture preferences of Americans ages 18-49.

We wanted to know whether the siloing that has been observed in Americans’ news environments is replicated when younger Americans are consuming entertainment media that often contains political content.

That matters, because popular influencers and entertainers who cross partisan boundaries have an increased ability to shape the political “vibe” discussed by Longwell. And an important finding from our survey is that many of the favorite creators and outlets ranked in the survey feature men and promote masculinity.
Pop culture is the diverse collection of cultural productions consumed by members of a society: films, television series, video games, art, music, comedy and the like.
We asked 741 Americans to name their top influencers, podcasts, comedians, musicians, video games, films and television series. We examined results by age and political party.

Respondents first identified which pop culture outlets they engaged with and then shared their favorites in each content category. The answers were diffuse, but trends are evident in the top three listed by people across political affiliations.
Both the Democratic and Republican parties have turned to influencers to reach voters – particularly young voters – who “don’t consume traditional political news.”

In our survey’s lists of favorite influencers, three creators who rose to fame staging viral stunts, interviewing celebrities and playing video games on YouTube and the live streaming platform Twitch dominated the list: MrBeast was No. 1 for Democrats, Republicans and independents. Republicans and independents ranked Kai Cenat in their top three, while IShowSpeed was No. 2 for Democrats and Republicans.

A similar pattern of the same names populating each list is evident in people’s favorite podcasts. “ The Joe Rogan Experience ” and “ Call Her Daddy ” were in all groups’ top three, while Republicans and independents also ranked the “ Tucker Carlson Show ” and “ This Past Weekend with Theo Von .”

Joe Rogan and Theo Von are comedians turned podcasters , whereas Tucker Carlson rose to fame as a right-wing pundit. “Call Her Daddy” is an outlier on our list insofar as it is hosted by a woman, Alex Cooper, and is known for frank discussions of sex and relationships.

The website Campaigns & Elections reported that in 2024 half of all registered voters surveyed who listened to at least one podcast per month said that podcasts had some influence on their vote . The site reported that in the 2024 presidential election, those podcast listeners favored conservatives.

Our survey helps to explain why. Rogan, popular with all three groups, has long voiced libertarian ideas and platformed right-wing politicians . Von occupies a similar space, and Carlson is conservative. Both are favorites not just of Republicans but also independents.
Political scientists and media scholars have demonstrated how comedy can influence politics. Our survey found considerable overlap among political partisans’ favorite comedians.

Dave Chappelle , creator of the boundary-breaking Comedy Central series “Chappelle’s Show,” topped the list for Democrats and Republicans and was the second favorite of independents. Bill Burr, known for comedy that is both cocky and aggrieved , was in the top three for Republicans and Democrats, while Shane Gillis, whose comedy The New York Times says “ fits into the evolving meaning of conservatism ,” was second and third for independents and Republicans.

Video games are another shared pop culture venue where Americans of different political affiliations are encountering one another as they play, via discussions with other players on Twitch and by participating in the comments sections of gameplay livestreams.

Researchers have demonstrated that young people, in particular, are exposed to diverse political views when engaging with one another in “ online participatory activities that are non-political in nature .”

For example, one study examined how a viral trend of “ building Trump’s wall” while playing Fortnite spurred political discussions both inside the game and in comments on gameplay videos and social media posts.

U. S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez demonstrated the political power of the medium in 2020 when she livestreamed herself playing the game Among Us, an online, multiplayer deduction game similar to the popular party games Mafia and Werewolf . Ocasio-Cortez playing the game with U. S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and prominent gamers was billed as a get-out-the-vote effort and earned 4. 5 million views.
In our survey of video games favored by people of different political affiliations, Call of Duty, Fortnite and Sims appeared on all three lists.

articles.title: Democrats are the unwitting beneficiaries of Trump’s immigration policies
articles.dek: In a 2025 investigation , The New York Times reported that officials in President Joe Biden’s administration, in the wake of Biden’s 2020 election win, had viewed rising…
paragraphs: In a 2025 investigation , The New York Times reported that officials in President Joe Biden’s administration, in the wake of Biden’s 2020 election win, had viewed rising immigration as “a distraction” best ignored so that the administration could concentrate political resources on more important economic matters.

Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was “wishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about.”

But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administration’s management of the U. S. southern border to win the 2024 election and enforce his immigration crackdown , the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.

Amid the rising U. S. cost of living , a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce , the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.
For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.

Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in 2006, 2007 and 2013 . Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.

In a February 2024 poll, 28% of U. S. respondents told Gallup that immigration was the country’s most important problem – matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period.

In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U. S. registered voters who identified immigration as the country’s most important issue fell from 14% in October 2024 to 5% in September 2026 .

Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have reduced the urgency of immigration , depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.
But this success is dubious. President Trump’s approval ratings on immigration are underwater.

In the RealClear Polling average from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10. 8%. In a recent Fox News poll , most Americans believe the Trump administration has “gone too far” in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.

Despite Republicans’ insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would raise wages and make housing more accessible , Americans are experiencing high inflation rates , slow gross domestic product growth and sour consumer sentiment .

Ominously for the White House, Trump’s negative 10. 8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at negative 42. 8% , negative 31. 7% and negative 27. 8% , respectively.
These dynamics bode well for Democrats’ midterm election prospects.

Republicans are now less concerned about immigration – what has been their greatest source of political energy and the left’s greatest political liability – as both parties’ voters are focused on other matters.

Despite the White House’s aggressive and frequently violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants , its proposal to end birthright citizenship , and its near closure of U. S. borders , even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the country’s top issue today than they were previously.
According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.

Remarkably, without Democrats’ endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey .
Democrats’ sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.

Before Trump’s 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U. S. , by highlighting that immigrants start more businesses , file more patents and commit fewer crimes than native-born U. S. citizens on average.

During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the praise and pity produced resentment among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.
Toward the end of the first Trump administration, Democrats began citing the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrants’ long-term settlement in the U. S.

Economists attribute to immigrants the bulk of U. S. population growth from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that continued immigration mitigates inflation and extends the solvency of Social Security and Medicare funds . Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, agriculture , food production and healthcare .
However, the benefits of these relationships for average voters tend to be diffuse and realized in the medium-to-long run. That makes them hard to recognize.

articles.title: We discovered an organism that lives at blistering temperatures – but what allows it to take the heat?
articles.dek: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in.
paragraphs: Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question for biologists like me is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move.

Organisms can adapt to survive in a wide variety of conditions, from salty water to extreme heat or cold and changing climates. Most eukaryotic organisms that have been studied with cell types similar to our own live at temperatures close to those of the human body , with an average of 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius).

Organisms thriving at temperatures higher than this range, known as thermophiles, could help directly answer what effect temperature has on the rules for life. These rules can help scientists learn more about where life could exist. In a study published in September 2026 , our research team identified a new thermophile that can survive at hotter conditions than any other previously recorded.

Eukaryotic cells , like the ones found in our bodies, contain organelles like nuclei and mitochondria . Eukaryotic organisms are reported less often than bacteria in extreme conditions, and based on observations from fungi at 140 F (60 C), scientists had theorized that eukaryotic life is not physically possible beyond 143 F (62 C).

In our new study, our team isolated and characterized a unicellular eukaryote , Incendiamoeba cascadensis , which is able to reproduce at 145 F (63 C). This finding marks the highest temperature yet recorded for eukaryotic life.
Our team found Incendiamoeba cascadensis in geothermal springs in Lassen Volcanic National Park , in Northern California, but we suspect it might also be found in other geothermal areas worldwide.

Like many amoebae – cells that change shape as they move – Incendiamoeba is a forager. It can move around in search of food and favorable conditions. It actively crawls at 147 F (64 C), but a few degrees more and it will enter a protective hibernation-like state.

While bacteria have been recorded living up to 212 F (100 C), it is unclear why eukaryotic cells are less amenable to high temperatures and other extremes. Many theories abound: Our cells have more protective membranes, including several membranes within each cell, surrounding their organelles. We also have complex molecular machinery that maintains our large genomes, and a dynamic cytoskeleton : a network of proteins that allows our cells to move.

Like other eukaryotes, Incendiamoeba has organelles, an active cytoskeleton and a relatively large genome, so what allows it to persist where others cannot? So far, Incendiamoeba has revealed that we don’t yet know which parts of eukaryotes are generally incompatible with high temperature.

As someone who investigates phenomena at the molecular level, I am always thinking about how molecules move and how motion increases with temperature. At higher temperatures, the velcrolike bonds holding proteins together can unfold, preventing them from performing their vital functions. Eukaryotes have evolved protein helpers called heat shock proteins , which detect protein unfolding and help refold them.

So, could Incendiamoeba simply have more of these helper proteins? Our team found that it does have a large reservoir of heat shock proteins, but making these proteins requires a lot of energy, and they must be folded themselves, so more helper proteins probably isn’t the full answer.

Incendiamoeba also has a unique set of protein building blocks that are good at holding proteins together. Yet this composition may only make up for the fact that proteins degrade more easily with increasing temperature.

We can look at Incendiamoeba’s genes, which turn on – or up – when temperature rises. Many of these genes are unknown. It is possible that one of these mystery genes is the key to its ability to withstand high temperatures. However, it is more likely, and in my mind, much more interesting, that there exists a symphony of small changes this organism has evolved, which confer its unique abilities.
By investigating Incendiamoeba and finding others like it, we can determine those changes and learn about the key principles for how life works on our environmentally diverse planet.

articles.title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road
articles.dek: Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping.
paragraphs: Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping. A few companies have begun testing early models on some limited routes in Texas and California . Simulations of automated fleets show the potential benefits of the technology: The vehicles could improve safety, enhance fuel economy and lessen transit times.

Truck makers and operators still have to solve some major issues, however, including how automated trucks will operate in variable weather and road conditions, and whether drivers should still be inside big rigs.
I am an engineer who studies human factors and transportation safety , and in my view, it is likely that automated trucks and human drivers will be working together for quite some time.

Fully automated trucks , which can drive on an interstate highway in good weather without human intervention, use a combination of AI, machine learning, computer vision, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. Torc , one company developing these vehicles, uses AI to combine data from multiple sensors and generate models that predict truck performance.

Data taken from modern big rigs that are equipped with certain technology such as automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping assistance systems indicate that fully automated, driverless trucks could reduce the number and severity of crashes. They could also save fuel and therefore cost by optimizing acceleration and braking , and by running multiple vehicles in a close-knit convoy or platoon . Driverless trucks could reduce parking needs as well as emissions from idling because they could run almost 24 hours a day and would not need to idle when they do park, which is common for regular rigs at truck stops.

Finally, automated trucks could help ease the ongoing driver shortage . Ironically, automation could make driving less stressful and less physically demanding, improving job satisfaction among drivers .
The main reason automated trucks are not common today is that they have difficulty operating in variable weather, under changing roadway conditions and alongside unpredictable drivers.

Automated trucks require sensors, radars and cameras that gather information about the environment around them to make decisions. However, snow and rain remain a problem for all automated vehicles , including cars, because they prevent the technology from “seeing” the roadway. Driverless taxi company Waymo, for example, only operates driverless cars in areas that get no snow.

Furthermore, any stretch of road where there may not be a predictable, clear surface and prevalent lines is difficult to handle . Imagine a construction zone with orange cones, narrow lanes and missing lane lines. Driverless car companies still try to avoid these areas . And, oddly, some research shows that automobile drivers tend to crash into driverless cars at a higher rate than they do cars piloted by people.
Given those challenges, companies are testing automated trucks on roads that lack complications.

For example, autonomous truck maker Aurora is operating large freight trucks on I-45 , a relatively flat and straight highway between Dallas and Houston. Rival Kodiak’s robotrucks are delivering sand to industrial sites in Texas over roads few people use. Few if any automated trucks are being tested in chaotic urban environments, given the pedestrians, bicyclists, traffic lights and elements of city traffic.
Some companies that were developing automated trucks have scaled back ambitions, changed direction or exited the market.

In 2023, Embark, TuSimple and Locomotion closed down . Waymo began to focus solely on cars . Other companies narrowed their focus to trucks that would operate only along a few dedicated routes between two large cities or manufacturing sites.
In my view, for years to come, automated trucks with AI-based controls will still require a driver.

The best technology will support a symbiosis between human and machine, where the person and the truck each do what they do best. A human would likely drive the truck across the “first mile” – the uncertain and crowded warehouse grounds and local streets to a highway. The driver would then stop using the steering wheel, gas pedal and brake and let automation take over. The human would take back control during the “last mile” to the truck’s final destination.

Research my colleagues and I conducted shows that human-machine interfaces that communicate between drivers and autonomous vehicles will be key. For example, a screen or heads-up display inside the cab would tell the driver how the technology is doing. Verbal messages or a vibrating seat could signal that the automation cannot handle a developing situation, and the driver would take over.

Developers will have to be aware of possible biases. So-called automation bias could lead to a driver who trusts and relies on the truck’s decision-making so much that they defer to it. Algorithmic bias could cause truck sensors to recognize certain groups of people on the road more than others, such as only detecting pedestrians of a certain size or shape.

The long-term vision is to have no driver, in part to lower costs. But driverless trucks do not seem to me to be practical on a large scale in the near future. It is more realistic to envision the driver and the automated truck as a team. Vehicle manufacturers, technology developers, regulators and drivers will need to work together to realize the benefits.

Shannon Roberts receives funding from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation, National Science Foundation, NYSEARCH, Sloan Foundation, and US Department of Transportation. She has previously received funding from Belron, GM, and Toyota Collaborative Safety Research Center.

articles.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
articles.dek: Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close.
paragraphs: Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024.

But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa.

It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “ news desert ” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U. S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets.

These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “ Good Morning Indian Country ” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston.

We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “ News Desert U ,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis.

Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U. S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report . Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years.
But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists.

Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work.

Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently.

In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers.

The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff.

“They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.”

Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines.
Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships.
Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.”
“People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.”

The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger.
Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000.
Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.”
Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo .

Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up.
“I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.”
NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership.

In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added.
